I'll work through each chapter systematically, applying the gate test carefully and respecting all authorized cuts.

---

**Ch 031 draft analysis**

The opening compression ("After a damp Highland summer and Switzerland no gayer, one drifted back in desperation to the Avenue of the Bois de Boulogne, where, for long summers to come, Adams hid in ignorance and silence") is a residue of the authorized removal of the Highlands–Switzerland–Paris shuffle, so any seam there is expected and not a finding.

The scholastic metaphysics, new psychology, and bicycle-rider analogy are all authorized digression removals. The draft compresses these into: "The new psychology had split personality into dualism and into complex groups like telephonic centres, proving that his normal thought was dispersion, sleep, dream, inconsequence; the simultaneous action of different thought-centres without central control. His artificial balance was acquired habit. He was an acrobat, with a dwarf on his back, crossing a chasm on a slack-rope, and commonly breaking his neck."

This compression jumps directly to conclusions without the logical bridge that led to them in the source. In the source, the bicycle-rider metaphor came first as an extended analogy, then the acrobat image emerged from that. In the draft, the acrobat image appears as the conclusion of a very compressed passage, but it still parses — a reader sees the acrobat as a metaphor for someone with artificial balance. The content stands.

The "Rigorous thinkers had at last fixed the law..." sentence — in the source this was attributed to a named tradition (Gibbon, Buckle, Auguste Comte). The draft drops the names but the sentence still parses as a general claim. Not a structural failure.

No structural failures found in Ch 031.

---

**Ch 032 draft analysis**

The authorized subplot removals include: "The Washington dinner spar over 'the American woman' and who's a 'failure'" and "The 'inertia of sex' essay." However, these are listed as authorized removals of subplots/digressions. But looking more carefully: the Washington dinner spar is authorized for removal, yet the *inertia of sex* content is only listed as an authorized digression for Ch 032 ("The 'inertia of sex' essay (bees, maternity axis, social statistics he wishes he had)"). The bulk of Ch 032's sex-inertia discussion is retained in the draft, so that's not a residue issue.

The dinner party scene is authorized for removal. The draft retains the dinner-table rhetorical device ("Sometimes, at dinner, one might ask one's liveliest neighbor...") and the reply ("Because the American man is a failure!"), but the actual dinner party with named guests and the specific rejoinder ("You are all failures!") is cut. That's authorized.

Now checking the sentence: "The woman seldom knows her own thought; she is as curious to understand herself as the man to understand her."

In the source, this appears within a passage explaining Adams's method of probing women's thought at dinner — it is part of an extended setup. In the draft it appears in a paragraph that begins "On this subject, Adams was conscious of having been born an eighteenth-century remainder..." The sentence still parses and makes sense in context. Not a finding.

Now: "He was studying the laws of motion, and had struck two large questions of vital importance to America—inertia of race and inertia of sex."

In the source, this paragraph opens with: "His own object had little to do with theirs. He was studying the laws of motion..." — "theirs" refers to professors and senators mentioned earlier in the source. In the draft, the preceding paragraph ends with the dinner-table anecdote about the woman answering "Because the American man is a failure!" Then comes: "Adams owed more to the American woman than to all the American men he ever heard of, and from the point of view of sex felt much curiosity to know how far she was right, and caught the trick of affirming that the woman was the superior. The cleverer the woman, the less she denied the failure..." Then several sentences about the woman's failures. Then abruptly:

"He was studying the laws of motion, and had struck two large questions of vital importance to America—inertia of race and inertia of sex."

In the source, this transition is bridged by: "On most subjects, one's opinions must defer to science, but on this, the opinion of a Senator or a Professor... is worth less than that of any woman on Fifth Avenue... Adams had here no occasion to deprecate scientific opinion, since no woman in the world would have paid the smallest respect to the opinions of all professors since the serpent. His own object had little to do with theirs." — This material was cut in the draft. The draft sentence "He was studying the laws of motion..." appears without any pivot. But does it parse? "He" refers to Adams, who is the subject throughout. It parses. However, it appears as a sudden re-entry into the analytical mode after the social observation paragraphs, with no connective. The source had "His own object had little to do with theirs" as the bridge. Without it, the shift is abrupt but not unparseable. A reader simply sees Adams returning to his analytical project. Gate test: a reader would not be *confused*, just reading an abrupt transition. Not a finding.

Now examining: "He had seen artificial energy to the amount of twenty or five-and-twenty million steam horse-power created in America since 1840, which had been socially turned over to the American woman, she being the chief object of social expenditure."

In the source, there was a parallel construction: "He had seen Mr. de Witte and Prince Khilkoff turn artificial energy to the value of three thousand million dollars, more or less, upon Russian inertia, in the last twenty years, and he needed to get some idea of the effects. He had seen artificial energy to the amount of twenty or five-and-twenty million steam horse-power created in America since 1840..." The draft drops the Russian de Witte/Khilkoff comparison but retains the American half. De Witte/Khilkoff are authorized minor character removals, so this is an authorized cut residue. Not a finding.

Now: "In Russia, no result had yet shown itself, but in America the results were evident."

In the source this reads: "In Russia, because of race and bulk, no result had yet shown itself." The draft drops the causal clause "because of race and bulk." Does this matter? The sentence still parses and makes sense. Not a finding.

Now checking the sentence about Holleben: "Suddenly Holleben received a telegram ordering him to pretext illness and come home, which he obeyed within four-and-twenty hours. No cause was guessed except the Kaiser's wish for a personal representative at Washington; breaking precedent, he sent Speck von Sternburg to counterbalance Herbert."

Holleben is an authorized minor character removal (Baron Hermann von Holleben). The draft retains Holleben by name — this is not a residue of an authorized cut, it's material the drafter chose to keep. The sentence parses fine. Not a finding.

Now: "The appointment of Michael Herbert counted for double the value of an ordinary diplomat: to reduce friction is the chief use of friendship, and in politics the loss by friction is outrageous. This personal sympathy prolonged Hay's life, and led directly to a revolution in Germany."

In the source, between "the small knot of houses that seemed to give a vague unity to foreign affairs opened their doors and their hearts, for the Herberts were already at home there" and "and this personal sympathy prolonged Hay's life" — the draft has cut the social opening of the houses. The referent "This personal sympathy" in the draft refers back to "The appointment of Michael Herbert counted for double the value of an ordinary diplomat: to reduce friction is the chief use of friendship." "This personal sympathy" — can a reader identify the antecedent? The preceding sentence says the loss by friction is outrageous — about friendship reducing friction. The antecedent of "personal sympathy" is not explicitly stated in the draft; the draft says Herbert "counted for double" due to reducing friction, but "personal sympathy" as the specific phrase has no explicit antecedent. However, a reader would understand "this personal sympathy" to refer to the friendship/relationship between Herbert and Hay's circle. Gate test: slightly awkward but not genuinely confusing. Not a valid finding.

Now examining the "broken pivot" test for the sentence in Ch 032: "The answer sounded singularly like the usual answer of British science" — this is Ch 031, not 032.

Let me check Ch 031: "The answer sounded singularly like the usual answer of British science, which had repeated since Bacon that one must not try to know the unknowable. Nothing was easier than to follow her advice, and turn to Thomas Aquinas..."

In the source: "The answer sounded singularly like the usual answer of British science which had repeated since Bacon that one must not try to know the unknowable, though one was quite powerless to ignore it; but the Virgin carried more conviction, for her feminine lack of interest in all perfections except her own was honester than the formal phrase of science; since nothing was easier than to follow her advice, and turn to Thomas Aquinas..."

The draft drops the contrast "but the Virgin carried more conviction, for her feminine lack of interest in all perfections except her own was honester than the formal phrase of science." Then goes straight to "Nothing was easier than to follow her advice." The source's logic was: British science said don't seek the unknowable → BUT the Virgin was more convincing than science → therefore follow her advice to ask Aquinas. The draft drops the middle term (Virgin more convincing than science) and goes straight from "British science said don't seek the unknowable" to "follow her advice." The pivot "but the Virgin carried more conviction" is cut, leaving "Nothing was easier than to follow her advice" floating without the reason why one would follow *her* advice rather than British science's advice to stop. This is a broken logical pivot: the draft presents a conclusion ("follow her advice") whose motivating contrast was cut.

Gate test: a reader would genuinely wonder *why* one follows the Virgin's advice rather than British science's equivalent advice, since the draft presents them as saying the same thing and then immediately says "nothing was easier than to follow her advice." The motivating distinction is lost.

This is a valid finding.
